review:
One of the best games of its generation, and a masterpiece singleplayer game of a kind they simply don't make anymore. Back when it was new, you needed a beast machine, plus it was only available on origin and gimped consoles, which is the chief reason it prompted really bad headlines in gaming magazines, with the memetic 'EA IS IN FINANCIAL CRYSIS!' being the one people are most likely to have seen, as, unfortunately, the game greatly underperformed.

Well, that was then, and this is now. For a very affordable price, you can get the entire crysis trilogy on whatever online PC platform of your choice, remastered, with all the money now going to Crytek itself, and no compromises having been made to the game to run on 30 FPS consoles, or accommodate low res monitors. Thanks to vast advancements in technology, the game looks better than ever, while requiring only a modest machine to max most everything out. Loadtimes used to be very slow, but are now all but instantaneous, even on slow harddrives, and all the various engine upgrades and ability to hold a high framerate finally, makes crysis 3, a game that was already intense compared to the games of its time, play even smoother, especially on a modern day 120-165hz monitor.

The music, voice acting, casting, and especially the story are all exceptional, as you'd expect from the sequel to crysis 2, but they went for a more action hero narrative, with some choice pieces of ham and actual drama, rather than pure post-apocalypse, and the main character gets a voice in this one, and by god, does he like to talk.

If you're a fan of meaty singleplayer action games that are completely self-contained, the way they used to be before DLC and games as services, then this should be a must own, same with crysis 2. Highly recommend.

[b]All good things come in threes, right?[/b]

Like the other games in the series, Crysis 3 Remastered is of course also part of the Crysis Remastered trilogy.
So now the only question left is whether the story will come to a worthy conclusion.

The story of Crysis 3 takes place several years after the events of Crysis 2, in which we were able to avert the threat of the extraterrestrial Ceph.
But the victory over the aliens was also the basis for the rapid rise of C.E.L.L, a private military organization that already played a major role in the second part.

[b]It's not over yet[/b]

The leader of the Ceph, the mighty Alpha Ceph, is still alive and New York, mostly in ruins, has become a veritable jungle where wild plants overgrow the streets and buildings.
C.E.L.L claimed victory over the Ceph, using alien technology to further expand their power and establish a military dictatorship.
[url]https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2911867304[/url]
As resistance against this vast organization grows ever more difficult, the rebels have decided to seize the only weapon that could decide victory or defeat.
Of course, we're talking about the nanosuit here, which developed independently through contact with Ceph technology.
And it is precisely in this suit that we find ourselves in the third part and, surprisingly, again as Prophet who supposedly died at the beginning of the second part.
I won't go into detail about the underlying events now, but I can tell you that, in the role of Prophet, we set out again for C.E.L.L. to bring down.

But first we have to get out of the hands of C.E.L.L. and luckily an old acquaintance from the first part's operations team comes to our aid here.
Psycho who rescues us from a transport pod we were frozen in.
However, as we are told in-game, he himself was cut out of his nanosuit. And this circumstance visibly bothers him more and more as the game progresses, so that the relationship between Psycho and Prophet is not always entirely uncomplicated.
All in all, I can definitely say that the quality of the story is roughly on the same level as Crysis 2. Sometimes the actual events seem confusing, but the staging is again very successful and is comparable to a good action movie and the short plot is still a good thing for the game in this case because there are no unnecessary fillers, even if the total scope thereby significantly reduced.

Apart from the plot and scope of Crysis 3, the game is very similar to the second part. This means that in the course of the game you are guided through relatively linear levels and are again confronted with a wide variety of opponents. Again there are partially open areas in which different approaches are made possible. Be it to attack the enemy position directly or to bypass it. Here, too, the abilities of the Nanosuit come into play, where we can, for example, either strengthen the armor or camouflage oneself temporarily in order to attack from an ambush.
So the basic gameplay hasn't changed, but the game has been upgraded with some useful things.
The most important innovation here is probably the bow, which, among other things, makes it possible to turn off the opponent silently.
The bow is also permanent equipment and can be selected separately with additional attachments, which in turn enable special attacks. In addition, the upgrade system has been revised again compared to Crysis 2.
A new addition is a hacker game that is essentially limited to pressing a key at the right time. Depending on the situation, hacking makes the gameplay easier, but in my opinion the whole thing is not really successful.

[b]The trilogy contains three undeniably solid titles that were just as good ten years ago as they are today.[/b]

Like the entire trilogy, Crysis 3 Remastered benefits from the heavily revised lighting and textures, which are significantly richer in detail. Everything now looks even clearer, sharper, has more depth and looks much warmer and more harmonious overall.
The story in Crysis 3 consists mostly of one-liners, a sometimes annoying side-kick and a greatly increased number of movie sequences and, in my opinion, doesn't quite come close to the two predecessors due to the short playing time, but for me it's from the remastered trilogy the best of the three games and the trilogy thus comes to a fitting conclusion.

In my opinion, the remastered trilogy is clearly the best available version of the games and comes with around 25 to 30 hours of playing time for fans of first-person shooters with a single-player campaign, which has not changed in terms of play, but has been significantly polished technically.

But since there are no new expansions or an extended story mode in the trilogy, one or the other may see it as a lazy cash grab.
Maybe you can see it that way and that's why I would also say that whoever already owns the games and / or has already played them must ultimately decide for themselves whether the technical revision of the trilogy justifies the price.

For my part, I had a lot of fun with the remastered trilogy and don't regret having bought it (cheaply).

Review date: January 16, 2023

I didn’t expect much from Crysis 3. I first played Crysis 2 about ten years ago on PlayStation 3, and recently I completed it again on Steam before starting Crysis 3. Even earlier, I played the original Crysis on PC when it first launched. So for me, this was more about revisiting the series than expecting something amazing.

But Crysis 3 surprised me in a very good way. It feels like the most complete and polished game in the trilogy. Everything works smoothly, and you can tell the developers really refined the experience. It’s a shame that when the game first came out, it didn’t get the attention it deserved.

In terms of gameplay, features, and mechanics, this is one of the best shooters I’ve played in a long time. The nanosuit feels more interesting here than in the second game. The ability to customize your suit and use different perks adds a lot of depth and variety.

One of the highlights for me was the bow. Using it while invisible is incredibly satisfying. I ended up playing almost the entire game with the bow, and it never got boring. It gives a unique feeling compared to standard weapons.

The game also offers good variety in how you approach situations. There are open areas, some light vehicle gameplay, and a small sense of sandbox freedom. You are not forced into one playstyle, which makes the experience more enjoyable.

Visually, the game still feels like a modern AAA project. Even today, it holds up extremely well. If Crysis 3 had been released last year, it would not feel out of place next to current titles.

The soundtrack is also outstanding. Playing with good headphones makes a big difference. The music by Hans Zimmer adds a lot of atmosphere. Listening to radio chatter during battles between aliens and CELL soldiers feels very immersive. The characters sound more alive and believable, not like simple background figures.

Performance-wise, the game felt stable on my system. The optimization seemed solid, and I didn’t run into any major issues.

Overall, Crysis 3 is the best game in the trilogy for me. It left me with only positive impressions, and I highly recommend giving it a try.

I sacrificed Laurence Barnes, the man I was, 
to become Prophet.[/h2]

Crysis 3 was one of the FPS games that got me into the genre when I was a kid, and replaying the Remastered Trilogy gave me a rather interesting perspective on it. It isn't as revolutionary as the original, nor is it as controversial as Crysis 2. Instead, it feels like a game trying to redefine what the series should be.

The biggest change is that Crytek deliberately steered the series back toward its roots. Compared to the tightly paced, highly cinematic New York of Crysis 2, Crysis 3 brings back larger combat spaces, more vertical level design, and encounters that encourage players to experiment and approach situations in their own way. The game is once again set in New York, this time transformed into a post-apocalyptic urban jungle, and it's easily my favorite artistic direction in the trilogy.

My favorite addition is easily the Predator Bow. It's just the perfect extension of the Nanosuit concept, so you get to fire while cloaked without breaking stealth, wich finally turns infiltration into a fully viable and sustainable playstyle while In the previous games, Cloak often felt more like a tool for repositioning. Crysis 3 is the first game in the series that truly makes you feel like a Predator.

The story doesn't really improve much over Crysis 2, but Prophet receives far more development and ends up being the only truly memorable protagonist in the trilogy. The campaign, around seven hours, is also quite short I must say, making Crysis the shortest game in the series. This really isn't the kind of length you'd expect from the finale of a trilogy. Many of its best ideas don't have enough time to fully develop before the credits roll. And while the finale certainly delivers on spectacle, the final boss itself is fairly underwhelming.

As for the Remastered version, I honestly didn't find the visual upgrade to be nearly as dramatic as I remembered. That said, the improved models, higher-quality textures, and lighting still hold up remarkably well today.

I think Crysis 3 strikes a solid balance between player freedom and cinematic storytelling. Although the series never got the chance to continue, it still serves as a respectable conclusion to the trilogy.

Here's hoping Crytek finally gets back to working on Crysis 4 instead of spending all its time on Hunt: Showdown. As great single player FPS games are becoming increasingly rare, this series deserves a sequel more than ever.

Crysis 3 picks up where the second game left off, not only in terms of its narrative but also with respect to its design. To that end, this is the best-looking, but most linear entry in the series.

I'd argue that Crysis 2 did a better job of providing a variety of tactical options for the player than the original game, and Crysis 3 continues that trend within its level design. But the feeling of freedom afforded by picking your own approach to completing objectives is somewhat suffocated here.

That's because Crysis 3 takes the hand-holding to a new level with a lot of sequences that feel like the game is playing itself, or levels where there's a character alongside you doing a lot of talking and pointing out what you need to do next. The presentation of everything is really good, but it just feels less special than the first and second games.

It doesn't help that the story is essentially a repeat of the first two games, with the same world-ending stakes, same threat of imminent nuclear catastrophe, and the same alien invasion. Even in this late entry, there is still next to no enemy variety, and while some sections of Crysis 3 definitely provide the greatest challenge in the series on the hardest difficulty mode, there are still huge sections of the game that can be trivialised by simply sprinting forward and activating stealth.

In true Crysis tradition, the final boss is pretty terrible. Overall, this gets a "Recommend" from me because I've enjoyed revisiting the trilogy with this remaster, but I think Crysis 3 may have some of the series' weakest points as well as a couple of its finest.

Crysis 3 is by far my favorite game in the series, I frankly think is quite underrated, the game provides a refined understanding from Crytek towards level design, stealth encounters, and overall, what makes the Crysis games enjoyable.

The level design is pretty varied, I wish it was a bit more open like in the first Crysis, but it's definitely an improvement over the second entry, each scenario feels different and they all have a number of cool set pieces to keep things from getting too stale.

Crysis 3 feels like the most refined version of what Crysis 2 started. It keeps the linear, cinematic structure but blends it with slightly more open combat arenas, bringing back a bit of that sandbox feeling from the first game, even if not fully.

Visually, this is easily the strongest entry in the trilogy. The mix between overgrown urban environments and futuristic architecture gives the game a distinct identity. The remastered version looks excellent without feeling artificially overloaded. Lighting, vegetation density, and environmental detail are well balanced. It’s visually impressive but not exaggerated for the sake of showing off.

Gameplay is smooth and responsive. The nanosuit feels more polished here. Combat flows naturally between stealth and aggression. The addition of the Predator Bow was a smart move — it reinforces stealth gameplay while still allowing aggressive options. It’s one of the most satisfying weapons in the trilogy.

That said, some mechanics from Crysis 1 are still missing. The deeper sandbox interaction never fully returned. The game gives the illusion of openness in certain areas, but progression remains mostly guided. It’s not a flaw, but it limits experimentation compared to what the franchise originally introduced.

The campaign is slightly longer than the previous two and feels more cohesive. Prophet is fully established as the central figure, and the tone is more consistent. It doesn’t reinvent the narrative formula, but it delivers a solid sci-fi shooter experience from start to finish.

Performance-wise, the remaster runs well if you have the hardware. It’s demanding, but not in a broken or poorly optimized way. It looks heavy because it is visually dense, not because it’s badly made.

Achievements are again well designed — no absurd grind, no forced multiplayer dependency, and everything can be unlocked naturally through progression and replay.

Overall, Crysis 3 Remastered is the most complete and visually polished entry in the trilogy. It doesn’t fully return to the experimental freedom of the first game, but it delivers a tight, satisfying FPS experience with strong atmosphere and smooth gameplay.

Crysis 1 brought an incredible evolution to the clumsy design principles presented in Far Cry, offering a blend of stealth and action with a dynamism reminiscent of the old immersive sims, albeit in a redundant, insubstantial, and empty open world (like a bare bones version of the subsequent Far Cry worlds), strangely dry and introspective given its vastness and visual exuberance.

All of this was enveloped by a psychotic and unreachable technical and technological excellence for its time.

Despite the hype (including within the game itself), Crysis 1 was far from being a bombastic and open action movie experience due to how quickly the suit's energy drains and your character's low resistance at any difficulty above normal. The game's enormous empty and purposeless space only worsened the experience, and the game only clicked for me when I started playing it like a hunter, embodying the Predator, with an entire jungle to hide in, ambushing unsuspecting soldiers in a precise and relentless manner.

Crysis 2 improved everything that worked in 1, enhanced the action, trimmed the fat, and transformed the experience into something more focused and linear, with impeccable pacing, well-designed arenas and levels that encompassed all the dynamism of the game's mechanics in a much more interesting and digestible way.

The fun was easier to reach. The excitement, the visual spectacle, more compelling than ever.

The game was transformed into a melodramatic Michael Bay-style action blockbuster full of epic gunfights and explosions, tempered by a solid core of stealth and dynamic difficulty systems.

The biggest novelty here is perhaps the ability to shoot without breaking invisibility, further reinforcing the fantasy of being a Predator. The return to "forests" and more open (yet purposeful) spaces makes the game experience bring elements from both previous games in an excellent and very satisfying combination.

Technically, I am still impressed with how they managed to make the game run impeccably on the PS3 and X360 at the time, without sacrificing almost any perceptible visual element. The game is still extremely beautiful by modern standards and refined in the smallest details, from animations, facial expressions, physics, particle effects, and so on. They even tried to enrich the context with some texts, audios and a mundane drama about a superhero who lost his powers and is frustrated because he can no longer break down a wall with his hands, but everything falls with the subtlety and elegance of a jackhammer five in the morning. 

It's loud, epic, immensely stupid and exactly what you want for the end of a trilogy.

This must be the result of applying an astronomical budget in a small scale game. You have a tight, polished experience, running smoothly and with due attention in all areas.

Crysis 3 is the one I haven’t played until now.

You play as Prophet, the guy that stole your body in the last game. After being put in a pod for 24 years, you’re saved by Psycho, that guy from the first game that was British and people liked. After giving you a gun, you follow Psycho and his resistance team so he can get you to fight CELL, who are still around and stronger than ever now that they provide unlimited energy via Ceph goo. 

And so you return to battle, using your Nano suit to fight humans and aliens alike, wondering why you’re only getting 40 fps in a game released in 2013 until you realized it turned RTX on by default and set it to high.

Crysis 3 is a little, --little-- bit of a departure from the series, moving so far away timeline wise from Crysis 1 and Crysis 2 to basically set up a new story. I mean, its a continuation of the first two, but now everything is all bad and dystopian and New York looks like a really pretty jungle with a dome around it. 

There’s a novel that came out alongside Crysis 3 called CRYSIS: Escalation that’s supposed to fill in a bunch of holes. But, like, I’m not going to read it? 

That being said, I do think I like this one the best. Crysis has always been this out of the way FPS series that EA published back in the day, and is now just published by Crytek proper with the Remasters. Its like those Medal of Honor games that came out in 2010 if they were actually good. 

The Nano Suit has been revamped a third time. Sprinting no longer costs energy, but you CAN get tired after a really long time of just sprinting. You can pick up upgrades for your nano suit and then spend those upgrades to get new powers, thing like longer stealth, heavier punch, being able to take a bajllion bullets before you die, scaring the shit out of everyone, things like that. If you use them a certain way then you get an extra bonus to said power boost. Its neat, I like it more than Crysis 2’s system where you stuck a straw in a Ceph corpse and stole their delicious Ceph juice for upgrades.

All of the Crysis usuals are still here. Modifying weapons on the fly to kill idiots better, jumping good, running good, running into people so hard that they splatter on the wall in a rag doll and just die instantly. 

There’s even more of an emphasis on pretending to be the Predator from Predator, especially now that you have a bow that doesn’t train your energy when you use it in stealth. Enemies aren’t as smart as they use to be, but they still happen to close in on wherever they think you are. They spend a lot of time in cover and spread out just enough that you can pick them off when you have the drop on them.

You can play the game as this mix of Doom 2016 and Batman Arkham Asylum. Lunging out and doing terrible things to terrible people before vanishing back into the brushes with your cloak. 
I like the mix up of a literal stealth archer and full blown heavily armed maniac. You CAN just play the game one way or another, stay in cover and let your energy recharge so you can go back to picking people off with your bow or just go in guns blazing.

But why would you do that? Do you hate fun? Are you stupid? 

There isn’t really much else I can say about Crysis 3 that I haven’t said about the last two games. I like the changes to the suit, the bow is fun, scaring the shit out of CELL troopers is fun, turning the Ceph into a nice milkshake is still fun. Its a good series, but I can understand why it didn’t pick up like some other late 00s to early 10s FPS games. 

Its science fiction but doesn’t go deep enough (at least without the novels, I guess) to satisfy codex readers and lore junkies. The shooting is fun but it doesn’t do anything different that other shooters haven’t done better. The stealth is fun but it never gets to the levels of other stealth games that came out around the same time. 

But I still had fun with the Crysis series. The original release had a multiplayer mode, but it looks like it shut down around a year ago. That’s sad, I liked the Predator mode. 

It has some problems, there’s a few plot holes and the characters just sort of exist most of the time. But Prophet and Psycho kind of carry the show, which is nice because you spend 90% of the game with Psycho and 100% of the game with Prophet, so it works out.
The game sort of peters out after the third last level, but that’s just how games used to go back in the day. They just sort of started sucking at the 80% mark. 
Crysis 3 gets 8.5 Prophets and Psychos kissing out of 10. 

We still don’t know what happened to Nomad.

Identity crisis seems to be normal in Crysis franchise, each game does it's own thing. This one is not any different. More dumbed down, some mechanics were removed and you're now supposed to be... stealthy. 

Crysis 2 was a game where you played with your entire arsenal, in here you're better off staying in the shadows. Yeah, you can go out and fight but you'll quickly find out that's a terrible idea. Natural regeneration takes longer, suit upgrade system was completely revamped - for better or worse - and you start off with the best weapon in the game early: the predator bow.

Don't worry, you get to keep this very bow till the end of the game so use it as much as you want.

From things I've liked:

- Predator bow is a cool weapon, though the only time you're required to use special arrows is way, waaayyy later into the game. Basically the last ending portion of it.
- Not as bullet sponge-y enemies as in Crysis 1, Crysis Warhead, or Crysis 2.
- Story is rich and explains a lot, but first hour is really rough in terms of pacing.
- Prophet and Psycho have fun banter between each other.
- Ending didn't feel as rushed as in Crysis 2.
- Less obnoxious timeskips than in Crysis 2.
- Slightly bigger maps but they're still very linear and most of the space is used for world building / environmental story telling.
- Overgrown sections in day time are still beautiful, even to this day.
- Nanovision is useless so you can finally ignore it and not be forced to hear the annoying suit voice telling you that it's on and off each time.
- Scanner now has better functionality which allows you to tag enemies, supply drops. It becomes integral part of the whole gameplay flow. You always wanna tag stuff, it makes traversing way easier.
- Alien weapons (alien weapons)
- Sniper got a thermal scope
- Shotguns actually have that "oompf" here now.

From things I've disliked:

- Sudden shift into more stealth-focused gameplay
- Initially your cloak runs out very fast and you can get spotted by enemies from 10km away, makes it [i]very[/i] annoying to get into the new play style.
- Enemies get alerted by your arrows if they spot it.
- Enemies and Turrets can spot you from very far away, even if you're in a bush. You need to explictly be behind something that completely blocks line of sight from all directions, otherwise you're alerting enemies.
- Doing stealth kills reveals you. Sure, there is an upgrade that stops that from happening but wtf, it's a stealth-focused entry. Why is it not a thing by default?
- Removal of Energy punishment for sprinting in trade-off for infinite sprint. The sprint is also slower.
- It's shortest entry in the Crysis franchise, parts of it felt like they were happening too fast, or were dragging out for too long.
- Night time areas and overall gloomy, dark areas ruined the art style of it and aren't as memorable as ex. the first time you walk outside.
- Extras didn't have concept art in it :(
- Extra lore about character, items, mobs and objects in the universe was told the "Bethesda" way aka. walls of text that is hard to read as the UI squishes it together into a small dialog box. I personally prefer if it's told via gameplay.
- "ACOG" scope still has broken sensitivity, same issue with Crysis 2.
- You have to constantly walk and retrieve your arrows. Missing feels extra painful due to it.

Overall, it's the weakest entry so far. If it wasn't for the gap-filling story and pretty fun combat then I would've left it with a negative review. Get it on sale and only play this after you have played every single Crysis franchise game - including Warhead - otherwise you'll be missing out on some context regarding Psycho.

If I were to rate them compared to other Crysis entries:

Crysis 2 > Crysis Warhead > Crysis 1 > Crysis 3

Now I am patiently waiting for Crysis 4. Good luck Crytek, hopefully you can manage to release it.

You know how sometimes there's a good game, but there's a big "but" about it? [b]Crysis 3[/b] is one of such cases. See, when [b]Crytek[/b] came out with the first [b]Crysis[/b], they had a unique idea. Sure, it was rather childish, but that's probably why people still remember the first game. Nobody else was crazy enough to make a game that would only run on high-end personal computers. Even though it was a time when everything else went multiplatform, [b]Crytek[/b] decided to make a PC-only beast—a monster to put even the most expensive hardware to the test. It was so crazy that the first [b]Crysis[/b] quickly became a meme, one that lives on to this day. Such an approach gave [b]Crysis[/b] a lot of press, made it famous, and—well—gave it an identity. You know, an identity. Like, everything on the market has its own niche: when you hear [b]HALO[/b], you think console-oriented stuff with heavy armor; when you hear [b]Counter-Strike[/b], it's a PC-oriented thing with quick deaths. The audiences? Drastically different. And [b]Crysis[/b]? The first [b]Crysis[/b] managed to achieve the most important thing—it found its own niche. It was a thing for the "PC mustard race" crowd, the same crazy hardware-loving enthusiasts.

That's why the transition to [b]Crysis 2[/b] felt... Well, not [i]bad[/i] (since, let's be honest, [b]Crysis 2[/b] was a fine game), but [i]wrong[/i]. Sure, [b]Crysis 2[/b] was one of the best-looking games on seventh-gen consoles, but at the same time, it was just that—a seventh-gen console-oriented title. Yes, the [b]Predator[/b]-inspired nanosuits were still there, and so was some freedom of approach, but all in all, [b]Crysis 2[/b] wasn't that different from other "shooters with powers." You know, [b]The Darkness[/b], [b]F.3.A.R.[/b]... That kind of stuff. It offered more freedom in single-player (like choosing between stealth and direct approaches) and even had fun multiplayer thanks to the suits, but the series lost its most important feature—its identity. Those huge maps and hardware-demanding visuals were gone. And for the third game? There were only two options: return to the roots [i]or[/i] stick with the changes. Spoiler alert—the series was published by [b]Electronic Arts[/b]. You can easily guess what they chose.

Going multiplatform means more money. Simple as that. That's why, for example, [b]The Elder Scrolls[/b] series got dumbed down after its third installment. [b]Bethesda[/b] managed to make a good port of [b]Morrowind[/b], but only the [b]Xbox[/b] was powerful enough to run it—and even then, it took creative tricks (like quietly rebooting the console in the background to save memory). Naturally, [b]EA[/b] didn't want to bother. They wanted something to sell across all platforms. Simple as that. The problem? We already had plenty of such games. The market was dominated by [b]Battlefield[/b] and [b]Call of Duty[/b]; [b]Medal of Honor[/b], while slowly decaying, was still around; and there were others, too. [b]Crysis 3[/b] desperately needed something to stand out. Did [b]Crytek[/b] find it? Well, yes. Kinda.

I already mentioned [b]Crysis 2[/b] being one of the best-looking games on consoles. Guess what? [b]Crysis 3[/b] looks even better—[i]a lot[/i] better, actually. And it's obvious [b]Crytek[/b] was proud of what they achieved. The game starts during heavy rain, and soon after, we see that instead of the Big Apple from the previous game, we get a new version of it—covered in vegetation. [i]Yes, vegetation.[/i] See, the lack of vegetation was one of the most shocking things about [b]Crysis 2[/b]—at least to those who loved the original. The first game was pure vegetation porn, while [b]Crysis 2[/b]? Just regular NYC. Now, in [b]Crysis 3[/b], [b]Crytek[/b] played it smart, presenting a ruined city (destroyed in the previous game) overgrown with plants. And it looked [i]fantastic[/i]. Sure, PC gamers still complained (don’t they always?), but on consoles? [i]Dude![/i] As someone who can't stand boring urban landscapes in games, I bloody loved what they did in [b]Crysis 3[/b].

What's even better, [b]Crytek[/b] didn’t stop there. They didn’t just add vegetation for show—the nanosuits were still a thing, and to differentiate the game, they leaned into stealth mechanics. Grass, for example, isn’t just grass here. Tall grass can be used for hiding [i]and[/i] spotting enemies—because cloaking won’t save you from disturbing the grass and alerting enemy snipers. In single-player, this brought [b]Crysis 3[/b] closer to the [b]Predator[/b] vibe it always chased, and multiplayer? Let’s just say it was a sniper’s paradise. And it was fun, you know? I played the multiplayer a ton back in the day and loved it. The problem was... [i]Why?[/i] What was the reason to pick [b]Crysis 3[/b] over, say, [b]Battlefield 4[/b]? And the thing is... there wasn’t one. Like any [b]Battlefield[/b] game since the third, [b]Crysis 3[/b]’s story was too short (just a few hours—the shortest in the series), and the single-player felt like an excuse. As for multiplayer? It wasn’t bad, and the vegetation mechanics were cool, but come on. [b]Battlefield[/b] had vehicles. And while [i]technically[/i] [b]Crysis 3[/b] had them too, they weren’t even close. In other words, [b]Crysis 3[/b] was just another [b]Battlefield[/b]-like game—and not even the best one.

Now, let’s talk about the remastered version. First things first: it looks [i]good[/i]. It’s a pretty boring upgrade overall, but the game totally holds up visually. Compared to other 2022 releases like [b]Overwatch 2[/b], [b]Warhammer 40,000: Darktide[/b], and [b]Shadow Warrior 3[/b]? It’s totally fine. The problem is (and if you’ve played the remastered trilogy, you saw this coming)—[b]Crytek[/b] removed the multiplayer. [i]Completely.[/i] That's it. There's no freakin' way to play multiplayer. Multiplayer here is no more! It ceased to be! 'E's expired and gone to meet its maker! It's a stiff! Bereft of life, it rests in peace! If you hadn't nailed it to the perch it'd be pushing up the daisies! Its metabolic processes are now history! It's off the twig! It's kicked the bucket, it's shuffled off its mortal coil, run down the curtain and joined the bleedin' choir invisible!! [i]IT'S AN EX-MULTIPLAYER!![/i] Now think about it. We have a typical [b]Battlefield[/b]-like game where nobody takes the single-player seriously—yet there’s no multiplayer. Like... [i]What?[/i] Sure, cutting it from the previous game was bad too, but here? Here it’s a joke. If you’ve played these games before, you can beat the whole thing in, like, 3–4 hours. And that’s it. Should I even say how wrong that feels? Playing the remastered [b]Crysis 3[/b] is like finding one of those dead games in your [b]Steam[/b] library—playing through the single-player and wondering how great the multiplayer must’ve been back when it was alive. The first [b]Crysis[/b]? At least its longer campaign made it worth the time. This? This is just sad. But hey, it looks good. Can’t argue with that—it looks good...

Crysis 3 picks up where the second game left off, not only in terms of its narrative but also with respect to its design. To that end, this is the best-looking, but most linear entry in the series.

I'd argue that Crysis 2 did a better job of providing a variety of tactical options for the player than the original game, and Crysis 3 continues that trend within its level design. But the feeling of freedom afforded by picking your own approach to completing objectives is somewhat suffocated here.

That's because Crysis 3 takes the hand-holding to a new level with a lot of sequences that feel like the game is playing itself, or levels where there's a character alongside you doing a lot of talking and pointing out what you need to do next. The presentation of everything is really good, but it just feels less special than the first and second games.

It doesn't help that the story is essentially a repeat of the first two games, with the same world-ending stakes, same threat of imminent nuclear catastrophe, and the same alien invasion. Even in this late entry, there is still next to no enemy variety, and while some sections of Crysis 3 definitely provide the greatest challenge in the series on the hardest difficulty mode, there are still huge sections of the game that can be trivialised by simply sprinting forward and activating stealth.

In true Crysis tradition, the final boss is pretty terrible. Overall, this gets a "Recommend" from me because I've enjoyed revisiting the trilogy with this remaster, but I think Crysis 3 may have some of the series' weakest points as well as a couple of its finest.

Waited for three entire games for Crytek to finally commit to the formula and even maybe improve it, but it simply didn't happen.

First one was just a glorified tech demo for me, they've shown some potential with the second one but it wasn't enough and this one is just a slightly better Crysis game but once again, without Crytek realizing the series' potential.

I don't understand why they went to great lenghts to prevent absolute freedom to the players. I'll be forever grateful to whomever it was that pushed for us to have unlimited stamina but I will never understand in general that why they limit certain suit powers and upgrades with only letting you use them in sets of fours. All this game --and to a point the entire series-- needed was one big skill tree, giving players the choice to invest in different powerups and just the ability to get said powerups [b]permanently[/b]. Forcing players to pick and choose between different skills in different situations is not only frustrating but also shows that they've picked the lazy option to balance suit powers, which is another decision I'll never understand as I don't think there is a need to balance [i]anything[/i] when it comes to the whole suit and its powers.

Why not let us be overpowered? Why not let us even break the game if it comes to that, as long as it can be fun? And as long as investing in those suit powers itself being the challenging part? Like, I can't even stop myself from imagining new and creative suit powers each time I go through a Crysis game but all they give us are the invisibility and the armor alongside upgrades to let those two last longer. I don't even wanna hear about the new bow because it's the same story; ammo is so scarce you don't even feel like trying stuff out with it unless push came to shove. It's a good addition to the arsenal but not a game changer unfortunately, it almost feels half baked and unfinished given how limited the things you can do with it are.

On a completely opposite note, I gotta give it to Crytek because they actually commited to something, even went the extra mile with it; the whole audiovisual sci-fi mumbo jumbo that plagued the entire series when it came to its presentation. Every briefing at the beginning of each mission consists of this almost incomprehensible holographic blueprint looking presentation with an absurd amount of hollywood style sci-fi visual clutter which makes everything very hard to understand for no reason at all. It's not like they can't pull off in-game or pre-rendered cutscenes either because there are plenty of those in the game and they are decent to their own right, but when it comes to giving actual information that matters about the mission you're gonna take, you've given just [i]gibberish[/i]. Truly baffling.

Despite all this however, I cannot at all call Crysis 3 a bad game. For people who care about the series' wacky and overstuffed lore or its soap opera-esque characters and story there is plenty to enjoy here. There are actually challenging and decently designed boss battles --especially compared to the first Crysis-- here and there, although I wish there were many more honestly, there is at least one decent addition to your arsenal which changes the overall gameplay loop ever-so-slighlty, unsurprisingly it's another fantastic looking Crysis game just as the other two titles and it serves as a decent conclusion to the whole series without a shred of unnecessary cliffhangers or sequel bait to be found anywhere which I find commendable in this day and age.

But as I said many times in different ways, it just wasn't enough for me. I find it so frustrating that they seemingly never cash-in on the overall potential the series holds. I still think there is a Bioshock or Prey caliber type of game hidden in Crysis and whatever happened/happening/will happen with the fourth one Crytek "teased" all those years ago, I hope they manage go without all the unneeded limitations they put upon themselves and make something other than the game equivalent of "Look how much foliage we can add to our game with huge open levels with so little to do! Who cares about level design anyways!"

Until then Crysis 3 and the series overall will stand as a bitter-sweet disappointment to me. None of the games were un-fun or a slog to playthrough and absolutely each game looked fantastic and especially 2 and 3 had this unmatched sense of scale they provide in terms of how they represent NY and all those belong to the [i]sweet[/i] part. However, I'll never stop being [i]bitter[/i] about the missed potential of the series until Crytek finally realizes it. Since I think Cryengine is at its lowest in terms of popularity, I don't think they have anything to lose in trying that so I'm still holding hope.

Recommended, though don't expect a massive visual upgrade for this one. Note that it doesn't feature multiplayer, and there are no cloud saves at time of writing.

The Remaster:
- Crysis 3 Remastered is the most visually similar remaster to its original of the three games. Most of the changes are quite subtle, with minor alterations to shadows and shading, and improved grass animation. Textures are largely the same, which is a shame as some of them look quite dated these days. Probably the biggest change is when running the water setting at very high quality, which enables planar reflections for bodies of water, a welcome improvement over the original screen space reflections. There are also ray traced reflections if you have the hardware, though you have to look a bit harder than the other games to see the benefits of these. DLSS is also included as with the other remasters.
- The game performs quite nicely, though very high settings are a bit heavy on the system so some users may want to reduce them to high. I've also heard that the game runs better than the original for a few people on older systems with lower settings, seemingly utilising the CPU more. The game also runs out-of-the-box on Windows 10, though the original only needed a minor fix to unlock high refresh rates anyway. That said, some people needed to install the lasted Visual C++ redistributables and / or set the game executable to Windows 7 or 8 compatibility modes to get the remaster to launch.
- There are a few quirks if you don't run default controls however, such as F being required for hacking even if you change your use key, and space being required for some key mashing events even if you don't use that for jumping.

Conclusion:
- For new players I recommend Crysis 3 Remastered, since you get the same single-player experience with the slightly updated visuals and quality-of-life improvements. For players of the original there's less on offer with this remaster, but I still recommend getting the Crysis Remastered Trilogy bundle, especially if it's on sale.

The Game:
- Crysis 3 returns to New York many years after the events of Crysis 2, with the city in ruins and overgrown. Gameplay is largely similar to Crysis 2, with the suit powers operating pretty much the same way. There are a few new additions to the arsenal, most notably the Predator Bow which can be fired when cloaked without draining suit energy, and has various arrow heads to choose from. There are also special ammo crates dotted around which allow more use of powerful weapons, plus some aliens now drop their weapons which can be used for short periods of time. There are a few new enemies and bosses, which add a bit more flavour over Crysis 2. Another new mechanic is hacking, which can be used to open weapon caches, disable mines, and turn automated turrets against enemies. It's a bit tedious since you have to time your clicks when moving dots reach their markers, but at least there's a suit upgrade you can get early on that completes some of it for you.
- The game is a little less cinematic than Crysis 2, with fewer characters that are focused on more closely, arguably making for a more engaging story. Most cutscenes can also be skipped now, which is handy for subsequent playthroughs. Music is once again excellent and fits nicely with the environments. Areas have been expanded to try and give a more open feel like the first Crysis, however in practise the gameplay is still quite linear and some areas feel a bit empty for their size, but you do sometimes get more freedom than in Crysis 2. Overall if you enjoyed Crysis 2 you'll probably enjoy Crysis 3, but don't expect a revolution in the gameplay, and be aware that it is a bit shorter too.
